description: We’re combining software development, UX design, and creativity to take on the Earth Information Jukebox challenge! Our goal is to turn NASA’s Earth visualisations into an interactive sound experience that makes Earth science more engaging and accessible.
summary:
What if almost everything we know about climate change came to us through pictures, and you couldn’t see them? 

For millions of visually impaired people, that’s the reality. NASA’s visualizations show the whole planet changing at once: oceans warming and cooling with the seasons, lightning flashing across storms, carbon dioxide building up in the air, and so much more. But that view is made for the eyes, and millions are left in the dark.

We’re Eggclipse, and through NASA’s Earth Information Jukebox challenge, we set out to give visually impaired people the same global view of our changing planet.

So instead of making one sound file to play once, we built EarthTunes, a tool that listeners can use and explore on their own. They can pick a dataset, hear how it changes over time, and follow along with a live description.

Sound can do more than describe a picture. It can reveal patterns the eye misses, like the steady rise of CO₂ or the pulse of the seasons. Climate change affects everyone, so understanding it shouldn’t depend on your eyesight. Our planet has a story to tell, and EarthTunes makes sure everyone can hear it.
details:
Earth Tunes turns NASA’s Earth visualizations into music. Each of its four “records” is based on an official visualization from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio and has its own voice. Sea surface temperature plays as flowing strings and a soft wordless choir that follows the seasons. Night lights become shimmering chimes that grow as cities light up from 2012 to 2023. Lightning seen from the International Space Station strikes as hand drums, one hit for every storm burst, and carbon dioxide plays as a deep drone that thickens where levels are high.

On the main page, you pick a dataset from the list, watch the NASA video in the middle, and learn what its colours and sounds mean in the panel on the right. Press Play, and the soundtrack changes with the data in real time. Higher notes mean more, whether that’s warmer water, brighter lights, more lightning, or more carbon dioxide. A live text description under the video tracks what’s happening on screen. The audio legend plays the scale from the lowest value to the highest. For carbon dioxide, an optional climate alarm uses a soft voice to mark the moments when the most carbon dioxide is in view.

In explore mode, the arrow keys move a sound cursor across the map, and each spot plays its own note. You can ask where you are, hear the value there (a real temperature for the ocean), or compare it with the average. The whole app also works from the keyboard, with shortcuts you can turn off and a “How to listen” guide for new users. You can adjust the volume and speed, loop a record, or expand the Earth view to full screen.

Our goal is to make NASA’s Earth data open to everyone, not just people who can see it. Visually impaired people get a second way in: they can hear patterns, growth, and sudden events while exploring the map by ear. Sighted users can catch what the eye misses; everyone, with or without sight, can experience the same data together.

We designed Earth Tune as a jukebox, with each dataset as a record you put on, so exploring climate data feels as familiar as choosing a song. Throughout the project, we balanced scientific honesty with musicality. Instead of mapping pixels straight to tones, we gave each dataset its own musical character and tuned it so small real changes can be heard without turning into noise. To do this, we measured brightness, warmth, location, and sudden flashes in every frame. We also matched ocean colours to NASA’s colour scale, so the sound follows real temperatures, not just shades on the screen.

We checked our results against known facts: the equator is warmest, city lights dipped in 2020 and grew about 27% overall, and lightning peaks every northern summer. Comparing frames side by side with our measurements also helped us remove false “lights” over Antarctica. We’re open about the limits too. The ocean data covers one year, carbon dioxide values are relative, and lightning has no exact dates.

To bring it all together, we used Python, NumPy, Pillow, and FFmpeg to turn NASA’s videos into data; JavaScript, HTML/CSS, and Tone.js to build the app and its soundtrack; and Git and GitHub to collaborate as a team. The violin and cello in the ocean record are real recordings from VSCO 2 Community Edition (public domain), and all other sounds are synthesized live in the browser from the data.
